scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The hand jive was invented in 1957 in Soho, London, at The Cat's Whisker coffee bar, where overcrowding prevented foot dancing.
Leon Bell is credited with its invention.
Filmmaker Ken Russell documented teenagers performing the dance in the crowded basement.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The hand jive was a practical dance created for crowded social spaces where traditional foot dancing was impossible.
It became a symbol of youthful creativity and social interaction in the 1950s, reflecting the energy of rhythm and blues culture.
It also served as a percussive accompaniment to music, turning hand gestures into a form of dance expression.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Ding Dong Daddy Hand Jive (https://archive.org/details/ding-dong-daddy-hand-jive)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The hand jive is performed seated or standing, often with a slightly crouched posture to bring thighs and shoulders closer for easier hand movement.

The basic sequence includes slapping the palms twice on the thighs, crossing palms over and under each other, pounding fists twice each, touching elbows with fingers one at a time, and hitchhiking gestures twice on each side.
Movements are synchronized to the beat, typically steady and syncopated, with no footwork involved.
Watch for Thigh Slap, Wrist Cross, Fist Pound.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Hand jive is danced primarily to rhythm and blues music of the 1950s, especially songs featuring the Bo Diddley beat—a syncopated rhythm with Afro-Latin roots popularized by Bo Diddley.
Instruments commonly include electric guitar, drums, bass, and vocals.
Listen for the electric guitar, drums, bass, vocals.
The pulse is 4/4.

The music features a steady, syncopated rhythm with a distinctive Bo Diddley beat, combining electric guitar riffs, driving drums, and soulful vocals that create a percussive backdrop for the hand movements.
